title: How the Antikythera Mechanism Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Antikythera mechanism, an ancient Greek geared astronomical device recovered from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera. They cover the 1900-1901 sponge-diver discovery and early recovery of statues, the wreck's likely origin as a grain ship converted to carry antiquities to Rome around 60 BCE, and later dives by Jacques Cousteau and an international team. They describe the mechanism's discovery in the museum, Derek de Solla Price's 1974 research and its reception, the Chariots of the Gods alien claims that discredited it, and modern CT scanning that revealed its gearing and inscriptions. They describe how it tracked the Sun, Moon, planets, eclipses, and the Olympic cycle, the metonic cycle, the proposed 205 BCE start date, candidate creators like Hipparchus and Posidonius, replicas, and comparisons to later geared devices. The episode closes with a listener correction about referring to autism as a mental illness.

segments.title: Opening banter and archaeology
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about their love of archaeology and Indiana Jones, then introduce the shipwreck off Antikythera and the field of underwater archaeology.

segments.title: Sponge divers discover the wreck
segments.summary: Sponge divers blown off course by a storm find the wreck near Antikythera around 1900-1901. A diver reports bodies, but the captain finds bronze statues, and the divers report the site to the Greek government, which funds excavation.

segments.title: Salvage, the wreck's history, and later dives
segments.summary: The recovered statues, including a bronze athlete and a philosopher bust, are displayed in Athens. The wreck is described as a large grain ship converted to carry antiquities to Rome around 60 BCE. Cousteau dove on it in 1950 and later international teams, including Woods Hole, returned to study it.

segments.title: Discovery of the mechanism in the museum
segments.summary: Item 15087, a corroded wooden-framed device resembling a clock face, was set aside among the statues. When it broke apart, museum director Spyridon Stais saw bronze parts with inscriptions and gear teeth.

segments.title: Derek de Solla Price's research and reception
segments.summary: Derek de Solla Price studied the device and, with Charalambos Karakalos, took X-rays. Price published Gears from the Greeks in 1974, but scholars were skeptical because precision gears seemed too advanced for that era. Price's correct theory of an astronomical mechanism was largely ignored.

segments.title: Chariots of the Gods and ufology distraction
segments.summary: Erich von Däniken's 1968 book Chariots of the Gods claimed aliens gave technology to humans, drawing popular attention but discrediting serious study of the mechanism.

segments.title: How the mechanism works
segments.summary: Modern CT scanning in the mid-2000s revealed the internal gearing. The device is a wooden box with a hand crank, gears with 15 to 23 teeth, hands for the planets, Sun and Moon, and dials on the back for eclipses and the Olympic cycle.

segments.title: Metonic cycle, inscriptions, and dating
segments.summary: The hosts explain the metonic cycle that keeps a lunar-solar calendar in sync, and how inscriptions in the device serve as a user's guide. Researchers using Babylonian eclipse records settled on 205 BCE as the likely start date.

segments.title: Possible makers and replicas
segments.summary: Candidates considered include Archimedes, who is excluded by his death in 212 BCE, Hipparchus, and Posidonius. Alexander Jones suggested Rhodes. About ten replicas have been built, including a watch-maker version and a Lego model.

segments.title: Other ancient geared devices and closing thoughts
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why the Greeks did not build further on the technology, mention Arthur C. Clarke's remark, and note a sixth-century CE geared calendar found in Beirut, the second oldest known geared mechanism.

segments.title: Listener mail: autism terminology correction
segments.summary: A listener points out that autism is a developmental disorder, not a mental illness, referring to an earlier episode remark. Josh and Chuck apologize and say they meant an autistic monk.
